=== CALL C0291 ===
Gareth: Hi, yeah, can you hear me alright?
Liam: yeah, can hear you fine
Gareth: Good. I'm Gareth. You're Liam, is it?
Liam: Yeah. Liam.
Gareth: Right. Er, so where are you calling from?
Liam: Walsall. Bloxwich, sort of.
Gareth: Oh right, Midlands. I'm Maidstone, in Kent. You look like you've had a long day, if you don't mind me saying.
Liam: Yeah, er, just come off nights. Did four on the bounce. Bit knackered, to be honest.
Gareth: What's the job?
Liam: IT technician at a parcel depot, up by junction ten on the M6. I keep the scanners going, the label printers, the PCs on the sort lines, the Wi-Fi. Anything with a plug, really, they ring me.
Gareth: Ha, right. I said on the form you looked like you worked somewhere like mine, but I think that was the fleece.
Liam: What do you do then?
Gareth: Civil engineer. Drainage, flood risk mainly. So if a culvert collapses, or a developer wants to build on a flood plain, that's sort of me. Bit of office, bit of home, bit of standing in a field in the rain in a hi-vis.
Liam: Right. So pipes and that.
Gareth: Pipes and that, yeah. Bigger pipes. What's the worst one you've had, on nights?
Liam: Er... Black Friday last year, a whole sorter line went down about three in the morning. Switch had died in the cabinet. Thousands of parcels backing up, managers all running round.
Gareth: What did you do?
Liam: Just swapped it. Had a spare. Took about twenty minutes. I let them think it was a bit harder than that, mind.
Gareth: [laughs] That's the trick, isn't it. I had a client ring me in a right panic once, flooding all over his car park. It was a blocked grille. Bloke with a rake sorted it. I still wrote a report.
Liam: Yeah, exactly.
Gareth: Is it all nights?
Liam: Rotating. Twelves. I do a lot of overtime, so it's fifty-odd hours most weeks. Pays alright for it. I want to get into network engineering though, days, proper money. Doing a CCNA, sort of.
Gareth: Sort of?
Liam: Half doing it. Hard after a twelve-hour shift.
Gareth: Fair. I did my chartership through work and the evenings were grim, I remember that. What do you do when you're not working?
Liam: Build PCs, mostly. Buy broken stuff off Marketplace, fix it, sell it on. Got a graphics card last week for like half what it should've been. Bloke didn't know what he had.
Gareth: Is it actually broken?
Liam: Fan was dead. Fiver for a new one. I'll sell it for about two-fifty.
Gareth: That's not bad at all. My son's nine, he's on at me for a gaming PC. I wouldn't know where to start.
Liam: Don't buy a prebuilt, they're a rip-off. Get one built, honestly, you'd save a couple hundred easy.
Gareth: Is that you offering?
Liam: [laughs] Could do. Walsall's a bit far for you, though.
Gareth: Bit, yeah. Do you follow the football at all?
Liam: Walsall. Loosely. They drew again Saturday.
Gareth: Charlton for me. It's always the hope that kills you.
Liam: We don't have much hope, to be honest.
Gareth: That's probably healthier.
Liam: Yeah.
Gareth: How are you finding all this anyway, the study?
Liam: Alright. Puzzle bit was fine. Mainly here for the money, if I'm honest.
Gareth: [laughs] At least you're honest about it. I think I'll probably—

=== CALL C0292 ===
Abena: Hello. Can you hear me?
Dean: Yeah, hiya. Yeah, I can hear you.
Abena: Good. I'm Abena.
Dean: Dean. Nice to meet you.
Abena: And you. So. Where are you?
Dean: Tipton. Black Country. Near Dudley, sort of.
Abena: I know the name. I'm in Thornton Heath, in Croydon. South London.
Dean: Ar, right. Never been down that way much. Only Palace for the football, once.
Abena: What do you do for work, Dean?
Dean: Er, press operator. Metal pressings, in Wednesbury. You put the sheet in, it stamps it, brackets and that for cars. Days and lates.
Abena: Do you like it?
Dean: Yeah. It's alright. It's steady, you know. Lads are sound. I don't get stressed with it.
Abena: That's worth something. I'm a practice administrator at a GP surgery in Norbury. Part-time, mornings, Monday to Thursday.
Dean: Oh right. My missus works in a care home. She's always on about trying to get through to the GP on the phone.
Abena: Eight o'clock. Everybody rings at eight o'clock, and then they're cross with the receptionist because there are only so many appointments. It's not the receptionist's fault, you know. I tell people that very plainly.
Dean: [laughs] Yeah, I bet you do.
Abena: I do. Erm, I do the rota and the letters, referrals, that kind of thing. Somebody has to know where everything is.
Dean: Ar. Kayleigh does all that at ours. Bills, forms. I'd lose 'em.
Abena: You would lose them?
Dean: Yeah, honestly. Ruby's school sent another letter home this week, trip form, and I forgot to sign it. Again. It's still in me coat, I think.
Abena: How old is Ruby?
Dean: Eight. She's Kayleigh's, but... she's mine, sort of, do you know what I mean.
Abena: Yes. Well, sign the form tonight. Put it by the kettle. That's what I'd do.
Dean: [laughs] By the kettle. Yeah, that's a good shout.
Abena: My son is twenty, at university in Leicester. He only rings when he needs money. So the forms never end, they just change.
Dean: [laughs] Ar.
Abena: What do you do at the weekend?
Dean: Weekend... er, fishing mostly. On the canal, or there's a pool near Himley. Caught a decent carp last Sunday. Fourteen pound, about.
Abena: Is that big?
Dean: For there, yeah. I put it back, though.
Abena: You put it back? After all that.
Dean: Yeah, you're meant to. It's just the sitting there, really. Nobody bothering you.
Abena: I understand that. I walk, Norwood Grove most days. And I have tomatoes in the garden. They're doing very well this year. Kwame, my husband, says I talk to them.
Dean: Do you?
Abena: Not out loud. ...Sometimes.
Dean: [laughs]
Abena: And then Sunday is church. I sing in the choir.
Dean: Sunday's my mum's, for us. Big dinner in Great Bridge, whole family.
Abena: What does she cook?
Dean: Roast. Beef usually, Yorkshires. Same every week.
Abena: Every week the same?
Dean: Yeah. I'm not, er, adventurous with food.
Abena: No? Then I would give you light soup and fufu.
Dean: Is it spicy?
Abena: It can be.
Dean: I don't go past a korma, me.
Abena: Then we would start you gently.

=== CALL C0293 ===

Daniel: Yeah, hi, I can hear you fine. I'm Daniel.

Daniel: No, you're fine. Where are you based?

Daniel: [laughs] Not many people say that. It's windy, mostly. So what do you do?
Chiara: So, erm, I was in brand partnerships for a luxury accessories house here in London. Hotels, influencers, collaborations, that kind of thing. And now I'm sort of... consulting. Freelance strategy work, for a candle brand at the moment. Taking a little break to think about the next step, to be honest.
Daniel: Right. That sounds like quite a big world.
Chiara: It's, yeah, it's a lot of lunches. Cioè, it's work, but it's a lot of lunches. What about you?
Daniel: What do I do? Erm, I run the trade counter at a builders' merchant in Lancing. So plasterers, chippies, people coming in at half six wanting timber and plasterboard. Quotes, stock queries. Not very glamorous.
Chiara: No, but that's so useful! Literally, everybody needs that. My husband and I can't even put up a shelf.
Daniel: You'd be surprised how many builders can't either.
Chiara: [laughs]
Daniel: I'm also doing an Open University course in the evenings. Social history. Slowly.
Chiara: Oh, that's amazing. I think I saw the books behind you, in the photo? I remember thinking, okay, he reads.
Daniel: Yeah, that's them. It's sort of something I never finished, so.
Chiara: Sorry, never finished?
Daniel: I started a degree and left after the first year. Money, mainly. So this is me having another go.
Chiara: I think that's really brave, honestly.
Daniel: Thanks. What's the best thing about London for you, after Turin?
Chiara: Erm, the galleries, the restaurants. I finally got a table at this place in Soho everyone is talking about, it took me three weeks. But the Italian food here, to be honest... no. Carbonara with cream. I can't.
Daniel: [laughs] I think I'm guilty of that. My mum's version has peas in it.
Chiara: Peas! No. Okay, I forgive your mum.
Daniel: Do you cook, then?
Chiara: Yes, every Sunday I make my nonna's agnolotti, by hand. It takes the whole afternoon. Tom, my husband, he's at a law firm in the City and he's very late every night, so Sunday is when we actually eat together. Is that what you mean?
Daniel: Yeah, that sounds really nice. I do the dinners at home on Thursdays and Sundays. I'm working through a Middle Eastern cookbook at the minute. Did a lamb thing with pomegranate last week that sort of worked.
Chiara: Sort of worked! That's how cooking is, no? Did your parents like it?
Daniel: My dad asked if there was any gravy.
Chiara: [laughs] Oh my God. That's my father with anything that isn't Italian.
Daniel: Do you travel much? I did a week in Porto last year.
Chiara: I love Lisbon! We did Lisbon, a little boutique hotel in Alfama. Porto I haven't done. Is it worth it?
Daniel: Yeah, I'd say so. It's cheaper than Lisbon, and the river's—

=== CALL C0295 ===
Gareth: Hi. Gareth. Can you hear me?
Daniel: Yeah, fine. Daniel. Nice to meet you.
Gareth: You too. Where are you?
Daniel: Worthing.
Gareth: Ah, south coast. I'm Maidstone. Practically the same road, apart from the A27 being a nightmare.
Daniel: [laughs] Yeah, it always is.
Gareth: I'll be honest, from your photo I put you down as being in the trade. Was I right?
Daniel: Sort of, yeah. I run the trade counter at a builders' merchant in Lancing. Timber, plasterboard, drainage bits. Half six start.
Gareth: Drainage bits! That's me. I'm a civil engineer, drainage and flood risk. So I'm probably the one specifying the stuff your lot can't get in stock.
Daniel: [laughs] You're the reason I get the phone calls, then. Some contractor ringing at seven wanting two hundred metres of a pipe nobody's heard of.
Gareth: Probably, yeah. Sorry about that.
Daniel: No, it's fine. It's the ones who order the wrong sheet sizes I can't stand. Had a bloke in last week, third time he'd done it. I measured it for him in the end.
Gareth: Fair play. And I noticed the books behind you. History?
Daniel: Yeah. I'm doing an Open University module, British social history. Evenings and weekends. Slow going, but I enjoy it.
Gareth: Nice. I'm a podcast man, mostly. I've just listened to one on the Tay Bridge disaster. Eighteen seventy-nine, the whole middle section came down in a storm with a train on it. And the thing is, the engineer had more or less not accounted for wind loading. Which, as an engineer, you listen to and think, yeah, that's the nightmare, that's the one that keeps you up.

Gareth: Yeah, we go to Charlton together. Three or four times a season. He's had a stroke, couple of years back, so it's a bit slower getting to the ground now. But we still go.
Daniel: Sorry to hear that.
Gareth: No, he's alright. Stubborn. What about football, do you follow anyone?
Daniel: Brighton. Go to the Amex with my dad a few times a season.
Gareth: Ah, well, you've got it good at the minute.
Daniel: Better than it was, yeah. I play five-a-side Wednesdays as well.
Gareth: Wednesdays! Me too. Work lot.
Daniel: Are you any good?
Gareth: I'm told I'm surprisingly competitive. I don't see it myself.
Daniel: [laughs] We're not competitive at all. We just sort of run about and go for a pint.
Gareth: That's the right attitude. I coach my lad's under-tens on a Saturday. They lost seven-one last week and nobody minded.

=== CALL C0299 ===

Abena: Yes. I'm Abena. Hello.
Gareth: Hello. Where are you?
Abena: Thornton Heath, in Croydon. You?
Gareth: Maidstone. Kent.
Abena: I put on my form that your office looked organised. The files with the project numbers.
Gareth: [laughs] That's very generous. Those labels were done by a graduate. If you looked inside, you'd be less impressed.
Abena: Then I'm glad I didn't look inside.
Gareth: Probably wise. What do you do?
Abena: Practice administrator at a GP surgery. Part-time. And you, the files are what?

Abena: What is a culvert?
Gareth: Sorry, yeah. It's basically a pipe or a tunnel carrying a stream under a road or a railway. When it blocks or falls in, the water's got nowhere to go, so it comes up over the road instead.
Abena: Like Brigstock Road when it rains.
Gareth: Probably exactly like that, yeah.
Abena: Is it a stressful job?
Gareth: Er, it can be, for other people. Clients panic. I sort of don't. I'm not sure if that's a skill or I just don't worry enough.
Abena: Both can be true.
Gareth: [laughs] That's what my partner says. She's a deputy head, Claire. She says I'm hard to read.
Abena: You are a bit.
Gareth: Fair enough.
Abena: I'm not complaining. In my work the calm ones are useful. At eight o'clock the phones go mad, everybody wants an appointment, and the receptionist who panics makes it worse for everybody.
Gareth: I can imagine. What's the worst bit for you?
Abena: People who don't do what they said they would do. Colleagues, I mean. Not patients.
Gareth: Ah. I should probably confess, I'm a bit last-minute with my timesheets.
Abena: How last-minute?
Gareth: Er... Friday afternoon. Sometimes Monday.
Abena: Monday is not acceptable.
Gareth: [laughs] No. I know.
Abena: Somebody is waiting on those numbers, you know. Payroll, billing. They're not doing it for fun.
Gareth: That's fair. I'll do it on time this week. Maybe.
Abena: Do it Thursday. Then Friday is free.
